parsed.same_study_reason: Both lists discuss stated-preference attempts to value farm-animal welfare, including WTP/WTA measures, cultured meat, welfare-neutral or suffering-free animals, and the conversion of valuations into per-kilogram welfare costs.

pairs.reason: Both question whether stated WTP measures isolate altruistic animal-welfare valuations rather than other motives. A2 states the broader construct-validity concern; B2 specifies product-quality expectations, food neophobia, naturalistic views, and concerns about preventing animal births in the cultivated-meat proxy.

Both argue that survey responses intended to measure willingness to avoid animal suffering are contaminated by other constructs or confounds. A2 is a general critique of the welfare-valuation measures, while B3 identifies particular hypothetical questions and certification-based alternatives.

Both concern the translation of meat-related valuations into a per-kilogram animal-welfare measure. A3 challenges the assumed edible-yield conversion; B2 challenges whether the one-kilogram conventional-versus-cultured-meat comparison measures altruistic welfare preferences at all.

Both challenge the use of stated WTP/WTA to identify external animal-welfare costs. A9 focuses on formal welfare-theoretic and interpersonal-comparability assumptions, whereas B2 focuses on non-altruistic preferences and beliefs embedded in the cultivated-meat comparison.

Both address the attempt to measure willingness to avoid farm-animal suffering through hypothetical valuation questions. A9 challenges the assumptions needed to equate those responses with external welfare costs; B3 emphasizes practical confounding in available elicitation methods.

Both say that responses in the valuation scenarios may capture aversion to features other than animal welfare. A11 supplies evidence from positive valuations of the welfare-neutral animal; B2 names extraneous preferences associated with cultured meat and animal non-birth.
